rows.question: How did our carriers' on-time performance change in Q3, especially on reefer?
rows.answer: Ridgeline's on-time performance slipped across the board in Q3: pickup fell to 93.1% from 95.4% and delivery fell to 91.8% from 94.0% [1][2]. Reefer was the weakest mode, with on-time delivery down to 87.2% from 92.5%, which the scorecard attributes to the September hurricane disruption and longer produce dwell times [3]. Reefer reliability also weakened on the carrier side, as carrier fall-off on reefer loads rose to 4.4% from 2.1% [4], and Ridgeline's reefer tender acceptance in the Southeast dropped to 78% in September [5]. Produce dwell is a cost and reliability issue: detention paid on produce loads rose to $41,800 in September from $23,500 in June [6], and an external survey reports 41% of reefer carriers now refuse loads from at least one shipper because of chronic detention [7]. Recommended actions include re-opening Q4 contract rates with the top 20 produce shippers [8] and enforcing signed BOL in/out times before paying detention, since only 62% of September produce detention was billed back to shippers [9][10].

rows.question: Summarize the broker transparency rule and what Ridgeline must change.
rows.answer: It says a broker must keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years, including shipper payment, carrier payment and accessorials, and produce it within 48 hours on request [1][2]. The rule takes effect February 1, 2027, with an August 1, 2027 date for brokers under 10 employees, and noncompliance can bring fines up to $10,000 per violation or suspension of operating authority [4][5]. For Ridgeline, the required changes are to remove carrier waiver clauses, store shipper and carrier payment amounts on the same TMS load record, and build a 48-hour records request process [3]; the library has no Ridgeline contract, TMS or help-desk documents, so the current state of these is unverified. Ridgeline's produce detention practice is a related exposure: it paid $41,800 in detention in September 2026 and only 62% was billed back to shippers because BOLs lacked signed in/out times [6][7].

claims.quote: Under the broker transparency final rule summarized here, a property broker must keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years. The record must include the shipper's payment to the broker, the broker's payment to the carrier, and any accessorial charges such as detention, layover and fuel surcharges.

rows.question: Under the food traceability requirement, what do we as a broker have to keep or provide on produce loads?
rows.answer: Under the food traceability requirement as summarized in the library, produce on the designated list (fresh tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens, melons, fresh-cut fruit) is covered [1]. Shippers and receivers carry the lot-level record duty, including traceability lot code, quantity, and origin and destination [2]. A broker that only transports the food does not have to keep traceability lot codes, but must be able to provide shipping documents within 24 hours when a shipper or receiver requests them during a recall [3]. Temperature logs are not required by the rule, though receivers may make continuous reefer logs a contract condition, so check produce contracts for that [4].

rows.question: What did the fall carrier survey say about reefer carriers shrinking or leaving the market, and why?
rows.answer: The fall 2026 Mid-South Carrier Pulse survey of 412 carriers (163 of them reefer operators) found that 22% of reefer carriers plan to reduce fleet size within six months and 9% are considering leaving the reefer market for dry van [1]. The reasons given by carriers planning to shrink were insurance premiums (64%), equipment financing costs (51%), and unpaid detention time (47%) [2]. For Ridgeline, this matches what we see internally: the Southeast lost about 6% of small reefer fleets since January, mostly owner-operators with one to five trucks, and 37 carriers were removed from the approved list in Q3, mostly for lapsed insurance [3][4]. Ridgeline's September reefer tender acceptance fell to 78% in the Southeast, so insurance-driven carrier loss and shrinkage are directly affecting our produce shippers' spot exposure [3][4].

rows.question: What general rate increases are LTL carriers planning for 2027?
rows.answer: Five of the largest LTL carriers have announced early-2027 general rate increases ranging from 4.9% to 6.5%, with a median of 5.9% [1]. Accessorial charges are rising faster than base rates, with liftgate fees up an average of 9% and two carriers adding a new residential delivery surcharge [2]. For Ridgeline, the practical read is that shippers tendering fewer than 50 LTL shipments a month will usually absorb the full GRI, while larger shippers typically negotiate one to three points off [3].

rows.question: What's driving reefer spot rates out of the Southeast this quarter, and what does it mean for our produce shippers?
rows.answer: Southeast reefer spot rates averaged $2.87 per mile in Q3, up 14% from Q2, while dry van rose only 4% on the same lanes [1][2]. Drivers included a produce push three weeks longer than usual [3], Hurricane Corinne stranding about 1,100 reefer trailers [4], and a thinning small-fleet base down about 6% since January [5]. Capacity is tightening further: 41% of reefer carriers now refuse loads from at least one shipper over chronic detention [7], and 22% of reefer carriers plan to shrink their fleets [6]. Detention is also a Ridgeline cost: three produce shippers accounted for 58% of September's detention bill [8], and Ridgeline paid $41,800 in detention on produce loads in September [9]. Ridgeline's September Southeast reefer tender acceptance fell to 78% [10], so the pricing desk recommends re-opening Q4 produce contract rates with the top 20 produce shippers, adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge line, and booking holiday produce 72 hours ahead [11]. Diesel at $3.94 per gallon, up 31 cents since July, adds surcharge pressure [12], and the desk expects spot rates to ease to $2.60 to $2.70 per mile in Q4 but not return to Q2 levels [13].

rows.question: Which of our produce shippers are driving detention costs, and how much are we paying?
rows.answer: Three produce shippers drove the bulk of September 2026 detention: Okefenokee Fresh Farms, Sunbelt Pepper Co., and Gator Grove Citrus together accounted for 58% of the September detention bill [1][2][3][4]. Okefenokee was the largest at $11,200 with 4.6 hours average dwell per pickup, Sunbelt Pepper $7,900 at 3.9 hours, and Gator Grove $5,150 at 3.4 hours [1][2][3]. Total produce detention paid to carriers was $41,800 in September, up from $23,500 in June, under a policy of 2 free hours then $75 per hour capped at $600 per stop [5][6]. Only 62% of September produce detention was billed back to shippers because the rest lacked signed in and out times on the BOL, so Ridgeline is absorbing a large share of this cost [7]. The pricing desk recommends re-opening Q4 contract rates with the top 20 produce shippers, which is the lever to pursue with these accounts [8].
